body.text: On Monday, the Opposition foreign affairs spokesperson Ted O’Brien appeared to say that the Paris Climate agreement was not legally binding. Or perhaps that the Coalition would exit it. One of the two.

Arguing against ratifying the EU-Australia Free Trade Agreement, he said it was unacceptable that the proposed deal with Europe “locks Australia in” to achieve its Paris commitments through a legally binding agreement.
That only makes sense if you don’t think the Paris Agreement is legally binding – or if you’re planning to exit it.
The Paris Agreement is a binding treaty the same way that a free trade agreement is.

Australia was one of 195 parties that adopted the agreement at the UN Climate Change Conference in Paris in 2015 – incidentally, under a Coalition government. It was duly considered by the Joint Standing Committee on Treaties, which recommended ratification. In 2016, then foreign minister Julie Bishop announced:

Will the Australia-European Union Free Trade Agreement be a different type of treaty? No. It also needs to be signed, scrutinised by the Joint Standing Committee on Treaties and then ratified (in the EU’s case, by the European Parliament). There’s no basis to view climate treaties as somehow less “binding” than trade ones.

A commitment to climate action is also included in Australia’s legally binding treaties with Fiji, Naoero and Tuvalu, to mention just three recent instances, with wording that is arguably broader – though less specific – than the EU agreement.

So, is the Coalition planning to exit the Paris Agreement? Both the Liberals and Nationals have reiterated their commitment to the climate change treaty in the context of One Nation’s policy that Australia should withdraw. However, O’Brien’s words could be interpreted as leaving a door open for this:
“Introducing legally binding climate obligations in the EU FTA risks eroding Australian sovereignty, by constraining the choices of future Australian governments.”

It’s not a view shared by all his colleagues. South Australian Liberal Senator Andrew McLachlan has said that the climate clauses in the EU trade agreement simply refer to honouring existing commitments– the same as in the UK free trade agreement signed by the Morrison government in 2021 and ratified by the Albanese government in November 2022.

A Monash student in the audience quizzed O’Brien how Australia can truly be part of the Pacific family if it ignores the region’s climate concerns. Polling consistently shows that climate change is considered a serious and pressing issue by most young people. O’Brien had framed his remarks by talking about what sort of Australia his young daughter will live in, urging that Australia take the opportunity to act with “ambition, urgency and courage”. But his comments left an impression that he was dismissing the issue that is top of mind for the next generation.
